requirement:
# REQ-2234: The analyzer does not work if SuppressSourceGeneration = true

Source: https://github.com/MessagePack-CSharp/MessagePack-CSharp/issues/2234

#### Bug description

The analyzer does not work if SuppressSourceGeneration = true. This has happened since version 3.1.1. It still worked in 3.1.0.

story.summary: The only source change is in TypeCollector.cs, in both member loops (properties and fields). After the mixed int/string key diagnostic is reported, the offending member is now skipped with `continue`. Before this, the code went on to `intKey!.Value` or `ContainsKey(null)` and threw. Members with a duplicate int or string key are now added to the member dictionaries only once, so `Dictionary.Add` no longer throws after MsgPack005 is reported. Alongside this, the change adds eight analyzer tests for `SuppressSourceGeneration = true` types, two execution tests, and a README section describing which diagnostics apply to suppressed types.
story.why: The issue says the analyzer stops working for `[MessagePackObject(SuppressSourceGeneration = true)]` types since 3.1.1. The change treats an exception thrown inside TypeCollector as the cause. Such an exception aborts the analyzer and swallows all its diagnostics. Nothing in the diff touches code that checks `SuppressSourceGeneration`. The fix is generic: it applies to generated types as well, as one of the new tests shows.
touches_beyond_requirement: README.md gains a new 'Opting out of source generation' section that documents analyzer behaviour, including MsgPack012, which no test covers.
An execution test project file adds a test type and two runtime tests; one of them asserts nothing about the suppressed type.
The duplicate-key and mixed-key guards also change behaviour for normal, non-suppressed `[MessagePackObject]` types.
story.confidence_overview: High: the duplicate and mixed-key guards in the property loop stop the crash, because the verifier would fail on an analyzer exception and the tests target exactly these cases. Low to medium: whether this is the actual 3.1.1 regression from the issue. No suppression-specific code changed, and several new tests (MsgPack004/015/003) may already have passed before the change. The field-loop edits have no direct test. The execution 'no formatter generated' test checks nothing.

findings.description: Claim C1 disputed: In the property loop, TypeCollector.cs line 1028 already guarded else if (stringKey is not null), so a null stringKey was never passed to stringMembers there (that unguarded else is in the field loop at line 1168). Furthermore, the named test MixedKeyKindsAreReportedWithoutAnalyzerFailure (SuppressSourceGenerationAnalyzerTests.cs lines 131-135) only tests an int key followed by a string key (isIntKey && intKey == null) and never exercises !isIntKey && stringKey == null.

Claim C13 disputed: SuppressedTypeRoundTripsThroughDynamicResolver (SuppressedSourceGenerationTests.cs lines 27-36) uses MessagePackSerializerOptions.Standard without asserting GeneratedMessagePackResolver.Instance.GetFormatter<SuppressedSourceGenerationType>() is null or passing a dynamic-only resolver. Because Standard includes SourceGeneratedFormatterResolver before DynamicObjectResolver, the test would still pass even if a formatter were generated for SuppressedSourceGenerationType, so it does not verify dynamic-resolver execution.

Claim C16 disputed: Wrong citation and mismatched test: C16 cites only TypeCollector.cs lines 1008 and 1148 (the mixed-key-kind continue statements), omitting the duplicate-key guards at lines 1023-1026, 1039-1042, 1163-1166, and 1179-1182, while its named test DuplicateKeysAreReportedWithoutAnalyzerFailureForGeneratedTypes (SuppressSourceGenerationAnalyzerTests.cs lines 147-166) tests duplicate int keys (hitting line 1023) and never executes lines 1008 or 1148.

No suppression-specific code changed. If the 3.1.1 regression was something other than this crash (for example, suppressed types being skipped before analysis), the issue is not fixed. The MsgPack004/015/003 suppressed-type tests may already have passed without this change, so they don't prove a fix.

The `continue` skips all later processing of that member, including the formatter-attribute and member-type checks. Other diagnostics for the same member (e.g. MsgPack003) may be hidden until the key is fixed.
The field-loop guards (lines 1148, 1163, 1179) are not exercised by any new test; all duplicate and mixed-key tests use properties.
NoFormatterIsGeneratedForSuppressedType asserts only that the resolver instance is non-null. It would pass whether or not a formatter was generated for the type.
The README states that MsgPack012 is reported for suppressed types, but no test verifies this.

Unlike the property loop at line 1028 (else if (stringKey is not null)), the field loop at line 1168 uses an unguarded else and calls stringMembers.ContainsKey(stringKey!) at line 1170. If the first serializable member is a field whose [Key] attribute has both intKey == null and stringKey == null (such as [Key(null)] or incomplete code during IDE editing, bypassing the non-first-member check at line 1145), stringMembers.ContainsKey(null!) throws ArgumentNullException and crashes the analyzer.

In both the property loop (line 1035) and the field loop (line 1175), hiddenIntKey++ is incremented unconditionally before checking !stringMembers.ContainsKey(member.StringKey) (lines 1039 and 1179). When a duplicate string key is skipped, hiddenIntKey has already advanced, leaving gaps in MemberSerializationInfo.IntKey across the retained stringMembers entries.
